X.title: A café's hot drinks and a coffee machine loan
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: A café recorded the maximum temperature, \(x\) °C, and the number of hot drinks sold, \(y\), on eight winter days.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Name the explanatory variable.

steps.working: The café is using temperature to explain or predict sales, so maximum temperature is the explanatory variable and hot drinks sold is the response variable.

pieces.mistake: Choosing the variable you are trying to predict. That is the response variable.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the equation of the least squares line for these data. Round the intercept and slope to two decimal places.

steps.working: With CAS, a linear regression of \(y\) on \(x\) gives intercept \(a \approx 239.82\) and slope \(b \approx -5.77\).
Write it with the variable names: hot drinks sold = 239.82 − 5.77 × maximum temperature.

pieces.mistake: Swapping the variables in the calculator, which regresses temperature on sales and gives a different line.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Interpret the slope of the least squares line in this context.
pieces.answer: On average, the number of hot drinks sold decreases by about 5.77 for each 1 °C increase in maximum temperature.

steps.working: The slope is the average change in the response variable for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable: on average, sales fall by about 5.77 drinks for each 1 °C rise in maximum temperature.

pieces.mistake: Leaving out 'on average', or saying sales 'are 5.77'. The slope describes an average change per degree.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: The correlation coefficient is \(r = -0.9984\). Find the coefficient of determination as a percentage, correct to one decimal place, and interpret it.
pieces.answer: 99.7%: 99.7% of the variation in the number of hot drinks sold is explained by the variation in maximum temperature.

steps.working: \(r^2 = (-0.9984)^2 \approx 0.997\), so 99.7% of the variation in hot drinks sold is explained by the variation in maximum temperature.

pieces.mistake: Saying 99.7% of the drinks are explained by temperature. The coefficient of determination is about the variation in the response variable.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the residual for the day with a maximum temperature of 15 °C, correct to one decimal place.

steps.working: Predicted value: 239.82 − 5.77 × 15 = 153.27. Residual = actual − predicted = 151 − 153.27 ≈ −2.3.

pieces.mistake: Calculating predicted − actual. A residual is always actual value minus predicted value.

pieces.text: The café borrows $12 000 to buy a coffee machine. Interest is charged at 6.6% per annum, compounding monthly, and the café repays $500 each month. Let \(V_n\) be the balance of the loan, in dollars, after \(n\) monthly repayments.

pieces.label: f.i
pieces.question: Write a recurrence relation for \(V_n\).

steps.working: The monthly interest rate is 6.6% ÷ 12 = 0.55%, so each month the balance is multiplied by 1.0055 and then reduced by the $500 repayment: \(V_0 = 12\,000\), \(V_{n+1} = 1.0055\,V_n - 500\).

pieces.mistake: Using 1.066 as the multiplier. The annual rate must be divided by 12 because interest compounds monthly.

pieces.label: f.ii
pieces.question: Find the balance of the loan after two repayments, correct to the nearest cent.
pieces.mistake: Subtracting the repayment before adding the interest. In this loan, interest is added to the balance and then the repayment is made.

pieces.label: f.iii
pieces.question: How many monthly repayments are needed to repay the loan in full?
pieces.answer: 26 repayments (25 of $500 and a smaller final repayment)

steps.working: With the finance solver (PV = 12 000, PMT = −500, I% = 6.6, compounding 12 times a year), N ≈ 25.8. So 26 repayments are needed, the last one smaller than $500 (about $405).

pieces.mistake: Rounding 25.8 down to 25. After 25 repayments about $403 is still owed, so a 26th repayment is needed.

X.title: Planning a school fair
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: A school is planning a fair. The activities, their durations and their immediate predecessors are shown below.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the earliest start time of activity G.

steps.working: G can start only when C, D and F have all finished. Their earliest finish times are 2 + 2 = 4, 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 and 2 + 4 + 1 = 7 days, so G's earliest start time is 8 days.

pieces.mistake: Taking the smallest finish time (4 days). An activity must wait for all of its immediate predecessors, so use the largest.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Write down the critical path and the minimum time needed to complete the project.
pieces.answer: Critical path A–B–D–G; minimum completion time 9 days

steps.working: The paths through the network are A–B–D–G (2 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 9 days), A–C–G (5 days) and A–E–F–G (8 days).
The longest path is the critical path: A–B–D–G, so the project takes at least 9 days.

pieces.mistake: Choosing the shortest path. The critical path is the longest one, because every path must be finished.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Find the float time of activity C.

steps.working: Latest start time of C = 8 − 2 = 6 days (it must finish by G's start at day 8). Its earliest start time is 2 days, so its float is 6 − 2 = 4 days.

pieces.mistake: Forgetting to subtract C's duration when finding its latest start time. Latest start time = latest finish time − duration.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Activity B is shortened from 4 days to 3 days. Find the new minimum completion time.

steps.working: A–B–D–G now takes 8 days, but A–E–F–G also takes 8 days, so the minimum completion time is 8 days (both paths are now critical).

pieces.mistake: Assuming the project gets 1 day shorter in every case. Check the other paths: once A–B–D–G drops to 8 days, A–E–F–G (8 days) limits the project.

pieces.text: Tickets cost $5 for adults, $3 for children and $2 for concessions. The matrices below show the ticket prices and the numbers of tickets sold on Saturday and Sunday. \[P = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \qquad N = \begin{bmatrix} 120 & 150 \\ 200 & 260 \\ 40 & 35 \end{bmatrix}\] The rows of \(N\) are adults, children and concessions; the columns are Saturday and Sunday.

pieces.label: e.i
pieces.question: State the order of the matrix \(PN\).

steps.working: \(P\) is \(1 \times 3\) and \(N\) is \(3 \times 2\). The inner numbers match, and the outer numbers give the order of the product: \(1 \times 2\).

pieces.mistake: Writing \(3 \times 3\) or \(1 \times 3\). The order of a product is (rows of the first) × (columns of the second).

pieces.label: e.ii
pieces.question: Find \(PN\) and explain what its elements represent.
pieces.answer: \(PN = \begin{bmatrix} 1280 & 1600 \end{bmatrix}\): ticket revenue of $1280 on Saturday and $1600 on Sunday.

steps.working: \(PN = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \times 120 + 3 \times 200 + 2 \times 40 & 5 \times 150 + 3 \times 260 + 2 \times 35 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1280 & 1600 \end{bmatrix}\).
Each element is price × number sold, summed over the ticket types: the total ticket revenue, $1280 on Saturday and $1600 on Sunday.

pieces.mistake: Multiplying element by element. Matrix multiplication multiplies each row of \(P\) by each column of \(N\) and adds the results.

pieces.text: At the fair, each hour 80% of visitors in the food area stay there and 20% move to the games area, while 30% of visitors in the games area move to the food area and 70% stay. Initially there are 100 visitors in each area. \[T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \qquad S_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 100 \\ 100 \end{bmatrix}\] where the first row and column refer to the food area, and \(S_{n+1} = TS_n\).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find the number of visitors in each area after one hour.
pieces.answer: 110 in the food area and 90 in the games area

steps.working: \(S_1 = TS_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 \times 100 + 0.3 \times 100 \\ 0.2 \times 100 + 0.7 \times 100 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 110 \\ 90 \end{bmatrix}\).

pieces.mistake: Reading the transition matrix by rows instead of columns. Each column shows where the people from one area go.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: In the long term, how many of the 200 visitors are in the food area?

steps.working: In the steady state the numbers moving each way balance: \(0.2F = 0.3G\) with \(F + G = 200\), so \(0.2F = 0.3(200 - F)\), giving \(F = 120\). (Or find \(T^n S_0\) for a large \(n\).)

pieces.mistake: Assuming the visitors end up split equally. The long-term split depends on the transition rates, not on the starting numbers.

X.title: A running club's times, members and savings
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: The 5 km times of a running club's members are approximately normally distributed with a mean of 28 minutes and a standard deviation of 3 minutes.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the standardised score (\(z\)-score) of a runner whose time is 22 minutes.
pieces.mistake: Dividing by the variance (9) instead of the standard deviation (3).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Using the 68–95–99.7% rule, find the percentage of runners slower than 31 minutes.

steps.working: 31 minutes is 1 standard deviation above the mean; 68% lie within 1 SD, so \(\frac{100 - 68}{2} = 16\%\) are above it.

pieces.mistake: Giving 32%, the percentage outside 1 SD on both sides combined.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Using the 68–95–99.7% rule, find the percentage of runners with times between 22 and 31 minutes.

steps.working: 22 minutes is 2 SD below the mean: 47.5% lie between 22 and 28 minutes.
31 minutes is 1 SD above: 34% lie between 28 and 31. Total \(47.5 + 34 = 81.5\%\).

pieces.mistake: Treating both sides as the same number of standard deviations.

pieces.text: The club's membership varies by season. The seasonal indices are shown below.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the seasonal index for spring.

steps.working: Seasonal indices for four seasons add to 4: \(4 - (1.15 + 1.05 + 0.80) = 1.00\).

pieces.mistake: Assuming the indices add to 1. With four seasons they add to 4.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: The club had 96 members in winter. Find the deseasonalised number of members.

steps.working: Deseasonalised value = actual ÷ seasonal index = \(96 \div 0.80 = 120\).

pieces.mistake: Multiplying by the seasonal index instead of dividing.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Interpret the summer seasonal index of 1.15.
pieces.answer: Summer membership is typically 15% above the seasonal average.

steps.working: An index of 1.15 means summer figures are typically 15% higher than the average for all seasons.

pieces.mistake: Saying membership grows by 15% each summer. The index compares a season with the average, not with last year.

pieces.text: The club invests $5000 in an account that pays interest of 4.2% per annum, compounding monthly. It adds $200 to the account at the end of each month.

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: Find the value of the investment after 3 years, correct to the nearest cent.

steps.working: Finance solver: N = 36, I% = 4.2, PV = −5000, PMT = −200, P/Y = C/Y = 12.

pieces.mistake: Entering PV and PMT as positive values. Money paid into the account is negative in the finance solver.

pieces.label: h
pieces.question: How much interest does the account earn over the 3 years?

steps.working: Interest = FV − total deposited = 13 329.17 − (5000 + 36 × 200) = $1129.17.

pieces.mistake: Subtracting only the $5000. The 36 monthly additions of $200 were deposited too.

X.title: A delivery business: routes, prices and customers
X.source: Original question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: A delivery company serves five towns, A, B, C, D and E. The roads between them and their lengths (in km) are: A–B 5, A–C 3, B–C 1, B–D 4, C–D 7, C–E 8, D–E 2.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Find the shortest route from A to E and its length.

steps.working: Compare routes: A–B–D–E = 11, A–C–E = 11, A–C–D–E = 12, A–C–B–D–E = 3 + 1 + 4 + 2 = 10.
The shortest route is A–C–B–D–E, with length 10 km.

pieces.mistake: Choosing the route with the fewest roads (A–C–E). Shortest means least total distance.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the total length of a minimum spanning tree for this network.

steps.working: Choose the shortest roads that do not form a cycle: B–C (1), D–E (2), A–C (3), B–D (4).
These connect all five towns, with total length \(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\) km.

pieces.mistake: Including A–B (5), which would create a cycle A–B–C. A spanning tree has no cycles.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain why the network has an Euler trail but not an Euler circuit.
pieces.answer: Exactly two vertices (B and D) have odd degree.

steps.working: Degrees: A 2, B 3, C 4, D 3, E 2. Exactly two vertices have odd degree, so there is an Euler trail (from B to D) but no Euler circuit.

pieces.mistake: Checking only whether the network is connected. Euler routes depend on the number of odd-degree vertices.

pieces.text: The company charges \(s\) dollars to deliver a small parcel and \(l\) dollars to deliver a large parcel. Delivering 3 small and 2 large parcels costs $34; delivering 1 small and 4 large parcels costs $38. This can be written as \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} s \\ l \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 34 \\ 38 \end{bmatrix}\).

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the determinant of the coefficient matrix.

steps.working: \(\det = 3 \times 4 - 2 \times 1 = 10\).

pieces.mistake: Calculating \(3 \times 4 + 2 \times 1\). The determinant subtracts the product of the other diagonal.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Use the inverse matrix to find \(s\) and \(l\).

steps.working: The inverse is \(\dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(\begin{bmatrix} s \\ l \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 4 \times 34 - 2 \times 38 \\ -34 + 3 \times 38 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\): $6 for small and $8 for large.

pieces.mistake: Multiplying in the wrong order. Solve \(X = A^{-1}B\), with the inverse on the left.

pieces.text: Customers choose between two delivery companies, Fast (F) and Swift (S). Each month, 90% of Fast's customers stay and 10% switch to Swift; 80% of Swift's customers stay and 20% switch to Fast. Initially Fast has 600 customers and Swift has 400. \[T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix}, \quad S_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 600 \\ 400 \end{bmatrix}\]

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Find the number of customers each company has after one month.

steps.working: \(S_1 = TS_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 \times 600 + 0.2 \times 400 \\ 0.1 \times 600 + 0.8 \times 400 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 620 \\ 380 \end{bmatrix}\).

pieces.mistake: Multiplying \(S_0T\). For a column state matrix the order is \(TS_0\).

pieces.label: g
pieces.question: In the long term, how many customers will Fast have, to the nearest whole number?

steps.working: At steady state \(0.1F = 0.2S\) with \(F + S = 1000\), so \(F = \frac{2000}{3} \approx 667\).

pieces.mistake: Assuming the split stays at 600 and 400. The long-term split depends only on the transition percentages.

X.title: Challenge: a car loan and a falling car value
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: Mia borrows $25 000 to buy a car. Interest is 7.2% p.a. compounding monthly, and she repays $500 at the end of each month. Let Bₙ be the balance after n months.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write a recurrence relation for Bₙ.

steps.working: Monthly rate 7.2/12 = 0.6%, so multiply by 1.006 and subtract 500.

pieces.mistake: Using 1.072 as the monthly multiplier.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Find the balance after 2 years, correct to the nearest cent.

steps.working: Finance solver: N = 24, I% = 7.2, PV = 25 000, PMT = −500.

pieces.mistake: Entering PMT as positive, which makes the balance grow.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: How many repayments are needed, and what is the final (smaller) repayment, to the nearest cent?

steps.working: Solving for N gives N ≈ 59.6, so 60 repayments are needed.
After 59 full repayments about $310.48 is owed; with one month's interest the final repayment is about $312.34.

pieces.mistake: Rounding N down to 59. A partial repayment is still a repayment.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Find the total interest paid.
pieces.mistake: Using 60 × 500 as the total, which overstates it.

pieces.text: The car cost $28 000 and loses 18% of its value each year (reducing balance).

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the value of the car after 3 years, correct to the nearest dollar.
pieces.mistake: Subtracting 18% of the original price each year (flat rate).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Write a rule for the value Vₙ after n years, and explain why it never reaches zero.
pieces.answer: Vₙ = 28 000 × 0.82ⁿ; each year the value is multiplied by 0.82, which is positive, so it approaches but never reaches 0.

steps.working: Multiplying by 0.82 each year shrinks the value geometrically, but a positive number times 0.82 is always positive.

pieces.mistake: Saying it reaches zero after about 5.6 years (100 ÷ 18). That is flat-rate thinking.

X.title: Challenge: forecasting seasonal sales
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of VCAA General Mathematics Exam 2

pieces.text: A shop's quarterly sales (in thousands of dollars) have seasonal indices Q1 0.85, Q2 0.90, Q3 1.15 and Q4 1.10. A least squares line fitted to the deseasonalised sales is: deseasonalised sales = 52 + 2t, where t = 1 is Q1 of Year 1. For this line, r² = 0.81.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Actual sales in a Q2 were 63 (thousand dollars). Find the deseasonalised value.

steps.working: Deseasonalised = actual ÷ index = 63 ÷ 0.90 = 70.

pieces.mistake: Multiplying by the index.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Interpret the Q3 seasonal index of 1.15.
pieces.answer: Q3 sales are typically 15% above the quarterly average.

steps.working: An index of 1.15 means Q3 sales are usually 15% higher than average.

pieces.mistake: Saying sales grow by 15% each Q3.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Forecast the actual sales for Q3 of Year 3.

steps.working: Q3 of Year 3 is t = 11: trend value 52 + 2 × 11 = 74.
Reseasonalise: 74 × 1.15 = 85.1.

pieces.mistake: Using t = 3 or forgetting to reseasonalise.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: The 70 from part a was for t = 6. Find the residual for this point.

steps.working: Predicted 52 + 2 × 6 = 64; residual = 70 − 64 = 6.

pieces.mistake: Calculating predicted − actual.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Find the correlation coefficient r.

steps.working: r = √0.81 = 0.9, positive because the slope is positive.

pieces.mistake: Giving 0.81.

pieces.label: f

steps.working: Forecasting far outside the data range assumes the linear trend continues, which may not hold.

pieces.mistake: Saying the r² value is too low.
